The growing intensity of Mr. Wopsle’s stare was so extraordinary, and he appeared to be considering so many things and becoming so bewildered, that I could not account for it. Long after he had risen into the clouds inside a great watch-case, I remained pondering it, still without understanding. I was thinking of it yet when, an hour later, I left the theatre and discovered him waiting near the entrance.

‘How are you?’ I said, shaking his hand as we turned along the street together. ‘I noticed you had seen me.’

‘Seen you, Mr. Pip!’ he replied. ‘Certainly I saw you. But who else was present?’

‘Who else?’

‘It is the most singular thing,’ said Mr. Wopsle, lapsing again into his bewildered expression; ‘and yet I could swear it was he.’

Growing uneasy, I begged Mr. Wopsle to tell me what he meant.

‘Whether I should have observed him immediately if you had not been there,’ Mr. Wopsle continued in the same distracted manner, ‘I cannot say for certain; but I believe I should.’

Without intending it, I glanced about me, as I was in the habit of doing on my way home; these mysterious remarks sent a chill through me.

‘Oh, he cannot be anywhere in sight,’ said Mr. Wopsle. ‘He left before I came off the stage. I watched him leave.’

With the grounds for suspicion that I possessed, I even distrusted this unfortunate actor. I feared some scheme to draw an admission from me. Thus, while we walked together, I looked sideways at him and held my tongue.

‘I had the absurd notion that he must have come with you, Mr. Pip, until I perceived that you knew nothing of his being there, seated behind you like a ghost.’

The earlier chill stole over me once more, but I determined to remain silent. Nothing in his words ruled out the possibility that someone had sent him to make me connect these allusions with Provis. Of course, I knew with complete and reassuring certainty that Provis had not been present.

‘You must think me strange, Mr. Pip; indeed, I can see that you do. But the thing is so extraordinary! You will scarcely credit what I am about to say. Were you telling me, I could scarcely credit it myself.’

‘Really?’ said I.

‘Indeed I could not. Mr. Pip, do you recall a Christmas Day long ago, when you were only a child, and I dined at Gargery’s, and soldiers arrived at the door wanting some handcuffs repaired?’

‘I recall it perfectly.’

‘And do you remember the pursuit of two convicts, and our joining it, and Gargery carrying you on his back, while I led the way and you followed me as closely as you could?’

But in yesterday’s bitter attack on Chantilly in the Musée, the writer made some shameful jokes about the shoemaker changing his name when he became an actor. He quoted a Latin line we have often discussed. I mean:

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

‘I had explained that this referred to Orion, whose name was once written Urion. Some sharp details connected with that explanation made me certain you would remember it. You were therefore bound to link Orion and Chantilly in your mind. The kind of smile that crossed your lips showed me that you had indeed made the connection. You were thinking of the poor shoemaker being torn apart by the critic. Until then, you had been walking with your shoulders bent; now I saw you straighten to your full height. That assured me you were thinking about how small Chantilly was. At that point I interrupted your thoughts to observe that, since Chantilly was such a very little man, he would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.’

Not long afterwards, while we were reading an evening edition of the Gazette des Tribunaux, the following paragraphs caught our attention.

‘Extraordinary Murders.—At about three o’clock this morning, people living in the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by a series of terrifying screams. These apparently came from the fourth storey of a house in the Rue Morgue, known to be occupied only by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After losing some time trying unsuccessfully to get someone to admit them, eight or ten neighbours broke through the entrance with a crowbar and went inside, accompanied by two police officers. By then the screams had stopped. But as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, they could make out two or more harsh voices arguing angrily, apparently somewhere above them. On reaching the second landing, they found that these sounds had also stopped, and everything was completely quiet. They separated and hurried through the rooms. Finally they reached a large rear room on the fourth storey. Its door was locked, with the key on the inside, and they forced it open. The sight that met them left everyone as horrified as they were astonished.

‘The room was in utter chaos. Broken furniture had been flung in every direction. There was only one bed frame, and the bedding had been pulled from it and thrown into the centre of the floor. A razor smeared with blood lay on a chair.

Soon we heard him call out.

‘How much farther do I have to go?’

‘How high are you?’ Legrand asked.

‘A long way up,’ the Black man answered. ‘I can see the sky through the top of the tree.’

‘Never mind the sky. Listen to me. Look down the trunk and count the branches beneath you on this side. How many have you passed?’

‘One, two, three, four, five—I’ve passed five big branches on this side, master.’

‘Then climb one branch higher.’

A few minutes later, his voice announced that he had reached the seventh branch.

‘Now, Jup,’ Legrand called, plainly very excited, ‘I want you to make your way out along that branch as far as possible. Tell me if you notice anything strange.’ By now, any lingering doubt about my poor friend’s madness had disappeared. I could only conclude that he had lost his mind, and I began to worry seriously about getting him home. While I considered what to do, Jupiter called down again.

‘I’m almost afraid to go very far along this branch—it’s dead nearly all the way.’

‘Did you say the branch is dead, Jupiter?’ Legrand cried, his voice trembling.

‘Yes, master, dead as a doornail—finished for certain—departed this life.’

‘What in heaven’s name am I going to do?’ Legrand asked, apparently in terrible distress.

‘Do?’ I said, thankful for a chance to get a word in. ‘Come home and go to bed. Come on now—be a good fellow. It’s getting late, and remember your promise.’

‘Jupiter,’ he shouted, paying me no attention at all, ‘can you hear me?’

‘Yes, Master Will, I hear you perfectly.’

‘Then test the wood thoroughly with your knife and see whether you think it’s badly rotten.’

‘It certainly is rotten, master,’ the Black man replied a few moments later, ‘but it could be much worse. I might manage a little way out along the branch on my own, that’s true.’

‘On your own! What do you mean?’

‘I mean the bug. It’s a very heavy bug. Suppose I drop it first; then the branch won’t break with only one Black man’s weight on it.’

‘You damned scoundrel!’ cried Legrand, looking greatly relieved. ‘What do you mean by talking such nonsense? If you drop that beetle, I’ll break your neck. Listen, Jupiter. Do you hear me?’

‘Yes, master. There’s no need to shout at a poor Black man like that.’

‘Well, listen carefully. If you go as far along the branch as you think is safe, and hold on to the beetle, I’ll give you a silver dollar the moment you come down.’
